1.pericope_label: I will extol thee, my God, O king; and I will bless thy name for ever and ever... Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable

schools.summary: Delitzsch identifies what is singular about the psalm — it alone carries the title tehillah, whose plural became the name of the whole book — and explains the Talmudic promise attached to it: not because it runs the alphabet, since Psalm 119 does that eightfold, nor because it celebrates God's care for every creature, since the Great Hallel does too, but because it unites both. Ellicott adds that in contemplating such greatness time ceases to be, and gives the literal form of the third verse, and for his greatness no search.

Calvin reports the same rabbinic saying, passes on Morison's guess that the psalm answers what the psalm before had asked, and draws two points of his own: that in calling God his King, David puts himself and every earthly prince in place, letting no distinction interfere with the glory due to God; and that we praise God aright only when filled with an ecstatic admiration of the immensity of his power, which is the fountain the praises flow from. Gill takes the King throughout for the Messiah, and insists he is no creature but God.

Clarke notes that the Hebrew and all the versions give the psalm to David, finds no occasion for it but simple gratitude, renders the third verse as saying that to his mightinesses there is no investigation, and reaches for Addison on the endlessness of the praise: through all eternity a joyful song I'll raise, but O, eternity's too short to utter all thy praise.

Henry makes praise a daily duty no day may excuse, hears three resolutions in 'for ever and ever' — David's own life, the church's use of his psalms, and eternity — and observes that praise belongs in ordinary conversation as much as in solemn devotion. Spurgeon sets the two kingships side by side, says praise is for all tenses, and holds that our praise of God shall be as eternal as the God we praise.

Augustine reads the title as praise to Christ, who came of David's seed and is yet David's Creator, and turns it into an argument about timing: begin praising now if you mean to praise for ever, since whoever will not praise in this transitory age will be silent when age upon age has come.

debates.question: Why has this psalm been singled out by tradition?

positions.summary: Because it unites two qualities that other psalms have only singly: it runs through the alphabet, and it celebrates God's care for every living creature.
The rabbis held it so high that whoever repeats it three times a day with sincerity of heart shall infallibly enjoy the blessings of the world to come — a saying reported without explanation.
Because David took a particular pleasure in it and sang it often; it was his companion wherever he went.

debates.question: What does the title 'of David' point to?

positions.summary: To Christ: praise to David himself means praise to him who came of the seed of David and is according to his divine nature David's Creator and Lord.
To David the author, on the authority of the Hebrew and all the versions, with no discernible occasion but gratitude.
To David writing after receiving what the previous psalm asked for, this being the new song he there promised to sing.

outliers.summary: Argues that praising God belongs in common conversation and not only in solemn devotion, since no subject of discourse is more noble, copious, pleasant, useful and unexceptionable than the glory of God.

Notices that the psalm was probably written when David's kingdom was flourishing, which is exactly why his addressing God as King matters: he gives himself and other earthly princes their proper place.

themes: I will extol thee, my God, O king; and I will bless thy name for ever and ever.
Every day will I bless thee; and I will praise thy name for ever and ever.
Great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised; and his greatness is unsearchable.

4.pericope_label: One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts... The Lord is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works

schools.summary: Ellicott reads the verbs as expressing indefinite continuance and corrects three words — the speaking of verse 5 may be singing, its object is the details of the wonders rather than wondrous works, the uttering of verse 7 is literally to pour forth in a stream, and the written text of verse 6 gives greatnesses in the plural, as Aquila and Jerome read it. Delitzsch marks that the self-description of God in verse 8 is taken over as the hundred and third psalm took it, with 'great in mercy' for 'abundant in mercy'.

Gill answers the terrible acts christologically, counting the flood, Sodom, Egypt and the Red Sea, and then the acts at the cross; measures the great goodness of verse 7 by its spring, the multitude it reaches and the benefits bestowed; and restricts the goodness of verse 9 to the special goodness of Christ toward all the chosen, Gentile as well as Jew — which is why he thinks the psalm belongs to gospel times.

Clarke distinguishes what is recorded in the word from what must be handed down by tradition, since providential dealings are innumerable; and on verse 9 he argues that there is not a soul out of hell not continually under God's merciful regards, so far is he from decreeing any man's damnation before creation, setting the verse squarely against what he calls the Molochian doctrine of the eternal decree of reprobation.

Spurgeon works verse 8 negatively: nothing in Jehovah is suspicious, prejudiced, morose, tyrannical or unapproachable, and being full of compassion he has no room left for forgetfulness or harshness — what an ocean of compassion there must be, since the infinite God is full of it.

debates.question: How wide is 'the Lord is good to all'?

positions.summary: Not providential goodness to all creatures but the special goodness of Christ, reaching all the chosen out of every nation, Gentile as well as Jew — which is what shows the psalm belongs to gospel times.

As wide as the words say: there is not a soul out of hell not continually under God's most merciful regards, and his son tasted death for every man — the verse standing against the doctrine of an eternal decree of reprobation.
As wide as the divine will itself, which tends towards the favour that gladly stoops to give and the compassion that interests itself on another's behalf.

debates.question: Should 'thy greatness' in verse 6 be singular or plural?

positions.summary: Plural — greatnesses — following the written text, as Aquila and Jerome read it, the parallelism decidedly favouring it.

outliers.summary: Draws a line between what Scripture records and what tradition must carry: God's creating and redeeming acts are in his word, but his providential dealings must pass from generation to generation, being in continual occurrence and therefore innumerable.

Fills out the terrible acts of verse 6 from both testaments — the flood, Sodom, Egypt and the Red Sea, then the darkened sun, the quaking earth, the split rocks and the torn veil that threw the centurion and his guard into a panic.

themes: One generation shall praise thy works to another, and shall declare thy mighty acts.
I will speak of the glorious honour of thy majesty, and of thy wondrous works.
And men shall speak of the might of thy terrible acts: and I will declare thy greatness.
They shall abundantly utter the memory of thy great goodness, and shall sing of thy righteousness.
The Lord is gracious, and full of compassion; slow to anger, and of great mercy.
The Lord is good to all: and his tender mercies are over all his works.

10.pericope_label: All thy works shall praise thee, O Lord; and thy saints shall bless thee... Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and thy dominion endureth throughout all generations

schools.summary: Ellicott's contribution here is textual and sceptical: the nun stanza has most probably dropped away, and the supplement the versions carry is only a variation of verse 17, unknown to the other ancient versions, rejected by the Jewish writers and suspicious in the one Hebrew manuscript that has it — though he concedes these arguments can hardly weigh against the improbability that one easy letter was left out of the original draft, or that the Greek translators would trouble to supply a verse for an arrangement they otherwise ignored.

Gill takes the works that praise God for the workmanship of his grace, locates the kingdom in the kingdom of grace rather than that of nature and providence — spiritual, not worldly, and lying within the heart — and sets its perpetuity against the Babylonian, Persian, Grecian and Roman monarchies, offering a second rendering of the phrase as a kingdom of all worlds or ages.

Clarke reads the saints as the compassionate ones who have partaken of the great mercy of verse 8 and bless God because they know he wills the salvation of all, against the bigots who can unfeelingly deal in the damnation of their fellows; and on the missing letter he refuses to believe the stanza never existed, calling its loss an unanswerable argument for the careless manner in which the Jews preserved the divine records, and printing the line the versions carry.

Henry separates praising from blessing — the works praise God as a building praises its builder, the saints bless him as children rise up and call their parents blessed — and contrasts the tottering thrones and withering crowns of earthly princes with an everlasting kingdom. Spurgeon answers the palace dedicated to all the glories of France with time, eternity and all space filled with the glories of God, and asks who can calculate the reserve forces of the Infinite.

debates.question: Was there ever a nun stanza, and is the versional supplement genuine?

positions.summary: There was: to say it never existed is false, since the alphabet is not complete without it, and its loss is an unanswerable argument for the careless manner in which the Jews preserved the divine records. The line the Syriac, Greek, Latin and Anglo-Saxon carry should stand.

The stanza has most probably dropped away, but the supplement is suspect — a mere variation of verse 17, unknown to the other ancient versions, rejected by Jewish writers, and doubtful in the one Hebrew manuscript that has it; though the improbability of an artificial composition omitting one easy letter tells the other way.

debates.question: Which kingdom does verse 11 speak of?

positions.summary: The kingdom of grace rather than that of nature and providence: not worldly but spiritual, coming not with outward observation but lying within the heart.
A kingdom whose pomp, power and perpetuity all outrun any earthly court — Solomon's and Ahasuerus's being glow-worms to its sun.
A kingdom identified with the one source of all force, mechanical, vital, mental and spiritual, with infinite reserve beyond what has been put forth.

outliers.summary: Turns the word for saints against a certain kind of believer: the compassionate ones bless God because they know he wills the salvation of all, unlike the dark, the gloomy, the hard-hearted, the narrow-minded bigots who never had that love shed abroad in their hearts and can unfeelingly deal in the damnation of their fellows.

themes: All thy works shall praise thee, O Lord; and thy saints shall bless thee.
They shall speak of the glory of thy kingdom, and talk of thy power;
To make known to the sons of men his mighty acts, and the glorious majesty of his kingdom.
Thy kingdom is an everlasting kingdom, and thy dominion endureth throughout all generations.

14.pericope_label: The Lord upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that be bowed down... My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord: and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever

schools.summary: Ellicott calls verse 14 a grand step in theology, since the first instance of divine majesty is sought in God's condescension to weakness — the heathen having seen with Ovid that succouring the fallen is king-like, without seeing that it is god-like; his note on the nearness of verse 18 is Tennyson's line, and on verse 20 he observes that guardianship of the good implies destruction of the wicked.

Gill narrows every promise in the section to the subjects of Christ's kingdom: not all who fell in Adam nor all who fall into sin are upheld, the eyes that wait are not those of beasts and fishes but of the Lord's people looking for spiritual food, and the hand opened is the hand of grace and not of providence. He passes on Aben Ezra's point that no mortal king can uphold all who fall.

Clarke reads the same verses at their widest — God the universal Father providing every creature the food suited to it and to every stage of life, so that all expect and none is disappointed — and closes on the two words for keeper and destroyer that stand a single letter apart, making of them a last invitation: so near is God a Saviour to those on the brink of destruction. Wesley adds that expectation is figuratively ascribed to the brute creatures.

Spurgeon reads verse 14 against the majesty of the verse before it, notes from the verb's form that the upholding is continuous, and dwells on whom God chooses — the fallen whom we shun, fallen women especially; and on verse 17 he includes the work most likely to be doubted, since in saving his people God has not shown mercy at the expense of justice but magnified his righteousness by the death of his Son.

debates.question: Whose eyes wait upon God in verse 15?

positions.summary: Every creature's: the young of all animals look up to their parents for food, and God is the universal Father providing the kind of food suited to each animal and to every stage of its life.
Only the Lord's people's, who look to him for their spiritual food as well as their bread; and the hand opened is not the hand of providence but of grace.

debates.question: Who are the fallen that God upholds?

positions.summary: The falling — those not able to keep their feet — whom God shores up as their prop, no man falling through his own weakness merely.
Not all who fell in Adam nor all who fall into sin, but the subjects of Christ's kingdom, whom no mortal king could uphold as he does.
Precisely those the world shuns, the fallen and the falling, since the Lord loves to reverse things and puts down the lofty while lifting up the lowly.
Human weakness as such — and it is a grand step in theology when the first instance of God's majesty is sought there.

outliers.summary: Suggests that it was the resemblance of verse 17 to the lost nun verse that caused the latter to drop out of the Hebrew text altogether.

themes: The Lord upholdeth all that fall, and raiseth up all those that be bowed down.
The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season.
Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing.
The Lord is righteous in all his ways, and holy in all his works.
The Lord is nigh unto all them that call upon him, to all that call upon him in truth.
He will fulfil the desire of them that fear him: he also will hear their cry, and will save them.
The Lord preserveth all them that love him: but all the wicked will he destroy.
My mouth shall speak the praise of the Lord: and let all flesh bless his holy name for ever and ever.
